 "The ergonomics are the best of any PRS model yet, by far": PRS Tekton T review
 Maryland’s finest enters the streamlined, contemporary, performance guitar market. Is the brand-new Tekton range a heavy hit?
Reviews
By
 Connor Flys 
Published
20 October 2026
 0 Comments 
 Join the conversation 
When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works .
 (Image credit: © Future/Olly Curtis) 
Guitar World Verdict
 Far from a mere phoned-in ‘modern’ rework of an existing model, the Tekton is all-new and feels it; it’s been put together with real care and attention to what today's guitarists need. If you've been waiting for a progressive, contemporary reimagining of the PRS blueprint, here it is.
 $2,899 at Guitar Center $2,899 at Guitar Center $2,899 at Guitar Center Check Amazon 
Reasons to buy
 + Fantastic-looking update of the PRS blueprint, with lots of very well-considered design features.
 + The Stylus pickups are really impressive, sounding clear and defined for both low and high-gain settings.
 + It plays absolutely superbly, and it’s clear that a lot of thought went into making the neck profile and the neck-to-body join as smooth as possible.
Reasons to avoid
 - The hard edge of the carved top against the picking arm is the sole ergonomic misstep.

 What is it? 
 One could argue that PRS didn't need to come up with “a guitar aimed at “the most discerning, technical players” (they're not just ' metal guitars '), contemporary musical styles and cutting-edge gear setups, as this has been the company's bread and butter for decades.
 Even the very first production PRS, the Custom 24 , remains immensely desirable among modern guitarists – decades since it was designed.
 So a more explicitly contemporary addition to the range could easily look like overkill; it needs to stand apart usefully from the Custom, rather than just packing in a bunch of gimmicks nobody asked for - or it mightn’t be worth the risk at all.
 Latest Videos From Guitar World Watch full video here: The company has decided to meet the challenge head-on, though, and here's the result – the Tekton range . There are four models, and this is the Tekton T – a six-string with the classic PRS vibrato.
 Can PRS win over the haters? | PRS Tekton T & Tekton SVN Demo - YouTube 
 Watch On 
 Specs 
 (Image credit: PRS) Launch price: $$2,899 | £2,899
 Made: USA
 Type: Six-string electric guitar 
 Body: Mahogany with figured mango top
 Neck: Maple, satin nitrocellulose finish, Modern D profile
 Fingerboard material/radius: Ebony, 16” radius
 Scale length: 25.5”/648mm 
 Nut/width: PRS composite, 42.8mm
 Frets: 24, jumbo, stainless steel
 Hardware: PRS Phase III locking tuners, PRS two-point vibrato
 Electrics: PRS Stylus bridge and neck humbuckers, 3-way pickup selector, Volume and push-pull Tone control (for coil split)
 Options: Fixed-bridge Tekton six-string, Tekton Floyd six-string, Tekton SVN seven-string
 Left-handed options: N/A 
 Finishes: Bloodstone Red (as reviewed), Slate Blue, Imperial Topaz, Black Tourmaline, Violet Tourmaline, Fuchsia Aura
 Case: PRS Premium gig bag (included)
 Contact:  PRS Guitars 
 Build quality 
 (Image credit: Future/Olly Curtis) Build quality rating: ★★★★½ 
 The Tekton shape is a slimmed-down, sharpened combination of the tried-and-tested Custom 24 and the offset Vela . It’s a really successful design; it still looks very much like a PRS, but modernised appropriately. Purposeful and elegant, it wouldn’t look out of place on a modern metal stage – but it needn't frighten away those with more classic tastes either.
 The back and sides of the mahogany body are painted a glossy metallic grey - a slightly odd-looking choice against the deep red top and satin black neck, but this varies by color choice.

Either way, there’s abundant contouring and a slim, sculpted bolt-on neck joint - worlds away from the oversized heel of a Custom 24, more reminiscent of something like Ibanez ’s All-Access Neck Joint. These are claimed to be the slimmest bodies and necks that PRS has ever put into production; the Tekton T is, indeed, wonderfully lightweight.
 (Image credit: Future/Olly Curtis) The ‘Shallow Violin’ carved top is mango wood, which PRS is liking currently; after the trees’ long and productive fruit-bearing lives are behind them, the mature wood is harvested as timber and it’s sustainable and high-quality – often beautifully figured too, as here.
 The six-string Tektons move away from the trademark 25” PRS scale length – it’s a Fender -familiar 25.5” instead. All models have 24-fret ebony fingerboards, and they all feature stainless steel fretwire too - de rigueur for many a modern guitar, and you can bet that there'd have been complaints otherwise.
 Hardware-wise, the solidity one expects from PRS is here in abundance. The Tekton T utilizes the company’s venerable two-point vibrato, and a set of its latest Phase III locking tuners; there's nothing to worry about whatsoever with any of that.
 Playability 
 (Image credit: Future/Olly Curtis) Playability rating: ★★★★½ 
 The Tekton T’s neck profile is a shredder's delight
 The contoured back and subtly offset shape allows the Tekton T to balance well and sit very comfortably. If there’s anything wrong with the ergonomics, it would be that the carved top creates a hard edge to the body where it meets the picking arm; it’s not as comfortable as a more traditional Strat -style elbow contour.
 However, the Tekton T’s neck profile is a shredder's delight. The maple is reinforced with hormigo, a dense hardwood, for extra stability, and PRS describes this neck design as ‘thin but substantial’, which does get the point across – fans of Jackson and Charvel should feel at home.
 The D-shaped carve feels nicely supportive, whether your hand is positioned for wide bends and vibrato or for fast scale runs. As you’d hope for this price, the finishing and fretwork are perfect too.
 (Image credit: Future/Olly Curtis) The PRS two-point floating vibrato is a tried-and-tested piece of hardware, and brings its usual functionality here. It’s great for expressive phrasing but, if silly noises are your bag, it can gargle and shriek with the best of ‘em too.
 If, like me, you’ve ever struggled to gel with the ergonomics of more traditional PRS models, you’ll likely find the Tekton range to be a dramatic improvement.
 Sounds 
 (Image credit: Future/Olly Curtis) Sounds rating: ★★★★★ 
 The Tekton range debuts a new pickup for PRS, too. Each model employs two Alnico 5-powered, modern-voiced Stylus humbuckers. It was decreed during development that these pickups should sound just as good with a digital-amp modeling setup as with a valve amp. That means a balanced frequency response, and a little less output - in theory, giving clarity and punch without sacrificing too much character.
 I fired up a contemporary digital rig (my small pedalboard designed to run direct, built around a Line 6 HX Stomp ), and cycled through some varied settings - majoring on more modern sounds, as that's the idea.
 (Image credit: Future/Olly Curtis) The split-coil sounds are excellent too – with more than enough punch and a useful change in character
 Right away, these pickups are exceedingly well-judged – crisp, clear delivery that lets your carefully-dialed tones shine through. The output doesn’t overpower a clean signal, and helps to keep higher gain tight and defined, with great string separation.
 It’s exactly what you’d want from a modern, two-humbucker guitar – sounding highly accomplished for anything from function-band sets to tracking modern metal riffs.
 The split-coil sounds are excellent too – with more than enough punch and a useful change in character that opens up even more versatility – from tight, defined single-coil rock tones to glassy cleans.
 (Image credit: Future/Olly Curtis) Verdict 
 (Image credit: Future/Olly Curtis) Price-wise, the Tekton range will sit near the other USA-built, bolt-on PRS range, the CE series – and it’s an ideal alternative, for those seeking a more overtly modern guitar.
 The ergonomics are the best of any PRS model yet, by far
 The new Stylus pickups fit their brief admirably, with superbly balanced, defined tones, while the ergonomics are the best of any PRS model yet, by far. It's versatile, too – a guitar that truly will work for a multitude of styles.
 This guitar truly does bring PRS's design philosophy right up to date, and it'll surely become a serious player in the high-end rock guitar market.
 Guitar World verdict: Far from a mere phoned-in ‘modern’ rework of an existing model, the Tekton is all-new and feels it; it’s been put together with real care and attention to what today's guitarists need. If you've been waiting for a progressive, contemporary reimagining of the PRS blueprint, here it is.

 Also try 
 PRS CE24 - $2,699 | £2,099 | €2,799 
The Tekton’s more traditional counterpart in the bolt-on PRS Core range, with the classic double-cutaway shape we all know. It’s worth trying to A/B them if you get the chance.
 Jackson American Series Soloist SL2 DX - $2,629 | £2,199 | €2,329 
If you want something more overtly metal-looking, the pointy headstock of the Jackson Soloist beckons. It’s neck-through, so it’s a little different to the Tekton – and it’ll play like lightning.

The 24-fret modern rock guitar market is Ibanez’s heartland. This Japanese-built Prestige AZ looks less purposeful than the Tekton, but spec-wise they’re very evenly-matched.
